newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan contractor becomes latest victim of bubble.
newsitem.headline: Japan contractor becomes latest victim of bubble.

text.p: Japan's troubled construction sector saw its second victim buckle under massive problem loans on Friday with a medium-sized contractor seeking bankruptcy protection from its creditors.
Tokyo-based Tokai Kogyo Co Ltd said it had decided to file for insolvency with a regional court after giving up its plan to rebuild its troubled business.
"The company has resolved to apply for court protection," a company spokesman told Reuters, without giving further details.
It was the second major insolvency filing by Japanese general contractors following Osaka-based Muramoto Construction Co Ltd which went under in 1993 with 530 billion yen ($4.69 billion) in debts.
But Tokai would be the first listed contractor to go under.

Tokai, listed on the fist section of the Tokyo bourse, was reportedly burdened with hefty debt of over 500 billion yen ($4.42 billion) and topped the list of Japanese builders which have guaranteed huge loans which may not be recoverable.

Tokai's shares were suspended by the Tokyo bourse after they fell on the news. Sales also emerged in shares like Tobishima Corp and Aoki Corp, as the news renewed market jitters over the fragile health of the construction sector, major casualities of Japan's bad loan crisis.

"Tokai's application will trigger further sales of shares of construction companies with poor financial profiles," said Hiroyuki Chikusa, an analyst at Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities and Economics.

Japanese government bond prices, meanwhile, rose sharply in Tokyo on the perception that Japan's economic recovery was still hampered by bad loan problems and the central bank would not be able to raise interest rates, traders said.
"That was a buy," said a dealer at a city bank's securities unit. "We had not forgotten the problems at construction companies. But at last, the problems are coming to light."
Japan's construction sector has been struggling to recover from the collapse of Japan's 1980s "bubble" of sky-high asset prices, which left them heavily encumbered with problem loans.
Builders led the bubble-era investment in property and real estate and also guaranteed loans by their real estate units.

The sluggish pace of Japan's economic recovery, coupled with lingering loan woes and a squeeze on public works spending, is putting heavy pressure on builders' earnings and has left any substantial turnarounds doubtful.

Tokai, hit by sluggish property sales and falling land prices, had tried but failed To win necessary financial support from all of its four major banks -- Hokkaido Takushoku Bank Ltd, Tokai Bank Ltd, Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan and Norinchukin Bank.
A Hokkaido spokesman said the bank, as a major lender to the company, would lead other lenders in hammering out a rehabilitation plan for the company.
On June 6, Tokai saw a net parent loss of 1.6 billion yen ($14.1 million) for the year to October 31, 1997, after a scant profit of 175 million yen ($1.54 million) the previous year. ($1=113 yen)
